introduction: On this Sunday, Hosea tells us that God desires mercy, not sacrifice. In the Gospel, Jesus calls Matthew the tax collector and eats with tax collectors and sinners, saying, Those who are well do not need a physician, but the sick do. Paul holds up the faith of Abraham, who hoped against hope. Let us come to Jesus, the physician of our souls.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, God desires mercy, not sacrifice. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may welcome sinners as Jesus did, and be a place of healing. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who feel excluded or despised: that they may hear Jesus call them by name. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the sick, and for doctors, nurses and carers: that Christ the physician may strengthen them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are faithful in outward practice but cold in heart: that God may teach them mercy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may follow Jesus at once when he calls, as Matthew did. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Merciful God, you desire mercy and not sacrifice. Heal our hearts, teach us to welcome sinners, and help us to follow your Son wherever he calls. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Follow me
reflection.body:
Hosea speaks of people whose love for God is shallow: "your love is like a morning cloud, and like the dew that disappears early." Then God says what he really wants: "For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings." Religious practice matters, but only when it flows from a heart that loves God and others.

In the Gospel, Jesus passes a tax booth and sees a man named Matthew sitting there. Tax collectors worked for the Roman authorities and were widely seen as traitors and cheats. Jesus says two words to him: "Follow me." And "He got up and followed him." The Church honors this Matthew as the evangelist whose Gospel we read this year.

Then Jesus goes to dinner with Matthew, and "many tax collectors and sinners came and sat down with Jesus and his disciples." The Pharisees are scandalized: "Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?" Jesus answers, "Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do." And he quotes Hosea: "But you go and learn what this means:" I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.

Jesus is not saying that sin doesn't matter. He is saying that he came precisely for sinners, as a doctor goes to the sick. If we think we have no need of him, we cannot receive his healing.

Paul shows us Abraham, who "Against hope... in hope believed," trusting God's promise even when it seemed impossible. Faith like Abraham's, and openness like Matthew's, are what God asks of us.

This week, admit to Jesus where you need healing, and let him come to you, perhaps in confession. And look at the people you tend to keep at a distance. Ask how you might show them mercy.
